notes:
I've put together notes for all seven verses, though only some kinds of sources turned up. Most of what I found comes from the older commentaries on biblehub.com, studylight.org and blueletterbible.org, plus Enduring Word (David Guzik). I had to stop searching before reaching preceptaustin.org, netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, oca.org or catholic.com. I found nothing showing real disagreement between denominations, and nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings, so those sections are left out. The commentators do disagree about when the psalm was written and about whether verse 4 describes the lying tongue or its punishment. Those disagreements don't follow denominational lines, so I've noted them under the verses where they come up.

Two of the sources below, the full Pulpit Commentary page and the Bible Hub chapter summary, have no citation markers. I read them in full, so the points from them are my own summaries with the link after each.

**Heading ("A song of ascents")**
- The Pulpit Commentary describes the debate over the title. One view links the psalms to temple steps (it says there's little evidence those steps existed). Another links them to the return from Babylon. It says most later scholars think they were songs pilgrims sang on the way to Jerusalem for the three yearly feasts. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/psalms-120.html
- In the same volume, R. Tuck instead reads them as "Songs of Heart-uplifting": each looks up to God out of some present distress. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/psalms-120.html
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: they were probably designed for the people going up to Jerusalem on the festival occasions, three times a year. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/120-1.htm
- The Geneva Study Bible takes "degrees" to mean "lifting up the tune and rising in singing." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/120-1.htm
- Bible Hub's summary says the collection opens here "far away" from Zion and later reaches the "peace within your walls" of Psalm 122. https://biblehub.com/psalms/120.htm

**v. 1**
- Who wrote it and when: Calvin admits he can't be sure but is "rather inclined to think that it was composed by" David. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/120-1.html Clarke (Methodist) thinks it appears to be a prayer of the captives in Babylon. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/brv/psalms/120-1.html The Pulpit Commentary lists guesses (the exile, or Samaritan opposition in Ezra and Nehemiah's day) but calls them "scarcely of much value." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/120-1.htm
- Past or present answer? The Cambridge-style note on that page says the psalmist calls to mind past answers to prayer as an encouragement to fresh prayer in his present distress. Keil and Delitzsch say the verb can also be read as confidence that the present cry will be answered. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/120-1.htm
- Barnes (Presbyterian) explains why he prayed: he couldn't answer or disprove the slander, so all that I could do was to commit the case to the Lord. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/120-1.htm
- An unnamed commentator on the same page advises "Silence to man and prayer to God are the best cures for the evil of slander." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/120-1.htm
- The Hebrew word for "distress" (*tsarah*) suggests being in a tight or narrow place. https://biblehub.com/psalms/120.htm

**v. 2**
- Matthew Henry: The psalmist was brought into great distress by a deceitful tongue. They forged false charges against him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/120-4.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary gives Sanballat's lies (Nehemiah 6:6–8) as an example. It says "deceitful tongue" literally means "a tongue that is fraud," and simply repeats the first line in other words. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/psalms-120.html
- Bible Hub notes that the word for "lying" (*sheqer*) is also used of idols, so lies take the place of God's reality. https://biblehub.com/psalms/120.htm

**v. 3**
- Pulpit: the question means "what will *God* give you?", that is, what punishment. "What will be added" echoes the oath formula "God do so to me, and more also" (1 Samuel 3:17). The tongue is addressed as if it were a person. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/psalms-120.html
- Guzik: The psalmist shifted from his prayer to God to speak to the false tongue of those who caused him distress. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-120/
- Tuck quotes Spurgeon: the slanderer can't be paid back in kind, because nobody can slander a slanderer, but God has threatened lying tongues and will carry out the threat. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/psalms-120.html

**v. 4**
- The main reading: this answers verse 3. Barnes: This is an answer to the question in Psalm 120:3. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/120-4.htm The Pulpit Commentary takes the arrows as those of a "Mighty One," meaning God, i.e., shall punish thee with extreme severity. https://biblehub.com/psalms/120-4.htm
- The other reading: Tuck says the verse could instead describe the lying tongue itself as arrows and coals. On balance he prefers the punishment reading. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/psalms-120.html Bridgeway takes both together: the insults pierce him like sharp arrows and burn him like red-hot coals, and he prays God's punishment will be just as painful. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/120-4.html
- The punishment fits the sin (Pulpit): a tongue that is a "sharp sword" (Psalm 57:4) is pierced by arrows, and a tongue that is "a fire" (James 3:6) is burned by coals. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/psalms-120.html
- Broom tree: Ellicott says "juniper" should be properly, broom. Travellers reported Bedouin making prized charcoal from it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/120-4.htm Barnes: such coals would be intensely hot, and would cause severer pain than if made from other wood. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/120-4.html
- Matthew Henry pushes it to final judgment: all that love and make a lie, shall have their portion in the lake that burns eternally. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/120-4.htm Gill notes that the Targum read the arrows as lightning from above and the coals as kindled in hell. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nrs/psalms/120-4.html
- A Bible Hub article connects the verse to Christ, who it says bore the piercing and the fiery wrath in the place of deceivers. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_use_broom_tree_coals_in_Psalm_120_4.htm

**v. 5**
- Where the places are: Guzik says Meshech was a distant place, far from the land of Israel, and Kedar was linked to nomadic tribes. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-120/
- Not meant literally: the Pulpit Commentary says Israel never lived among the Moschi of Cappadocia or the Arabian Kedarites. The names stand for hostile, barbarous neighbours, possibly the Samaritans and Ammonites. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/psalms-120.html Matthew Henry suggests Perhaps Saul's court was the Mesech and Kedar in which David dwelt. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_120.cfm Barnes: to dwell among slanderers was like dwelling among barbarians and savages. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/lit/psalms/120-5.html
- How Guzik applies it: the psalmist felt like a sojourner among the ungodly, never truly at home. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-120/ A Biblical Illustrator sermon takes comfort from the word "sojourn": it is only a tent I dwell in, and that will come down by and by. https://biblehub.com/sermons/psalms/120-5.htm
- A different text tradition: the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) and the Catholic Douay-Rheims read "Woe is me, that my sojourning is prolonged!" https://biblehub.com/psalms/120-5.htm Henry reports this reading as the exile's longing to get home to God's altars. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_120.cfm
- Early church: in his *Apology* (on newadvent.org), Rufinus reports a view, credited to Jerome writing under someone else's name, that used this reading as evidence that souls were cast down into this vale of tears, this place of our mournful pilgrimage. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/27051.htm

**v. 6**
- Pulpit: "those who hate peace" are the tribes symbolised in verse 5, the neighbours bordering Judea, who were nearly always at war with Israel. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/psalms-120.html
- Guzik: The psalmist ached because he lived among the ungodly and was distant from Israel and its people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-120/
- The Douay-Rheims renders the verse "My soul hath been long a sojourner." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rhe/psalms/120-5.html

**v. 7**
- Pulpit: the Hebrew is literally "I am peace," but the meaning is "I am for peace." "When I speak" means when I speak to them of peace, and they are set on constant hostility. The commentary mentions the Samaritans' offer to help build the temple (Ezra 4:2), which may have been insincere. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/psalms-120.html
- Bible Hub: *shalom* means wholeness, not just a truce. It links the verse to Romans 12:18 (live at peace with everyone) and advises working for peace without giving up the truth. https://biblehub.com/psalms/120.htm
- The Douay-Rheims reads: "With them that hated peace I was peaceable: when I spoke to them they fought against me without cause." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rhe/psalms/120-5.html
- Practical comfort from the Pulpit homilies: living among hostile people is part of our earthly lot. It won't last long, it trains our character, and God remains our refuge. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/psalms-120.html

**Not found:** the netbible.org translators' notes, Augustine's own commentary on this psalm, Catholic or Orthodox commentary beyond the Douay-Rheims wording, any distinctively Baptist, Lutheran or Pentecostal reading that differs from the others, and any discussion of popular modern teaching on this psalm.
